list.listitem: There is insufficient evidence to recommend screening non-pregnant asymptomatic adults for thyroid dysfunction (USPSTF I recommendation). C

When thyroiditis is clinically suspected, order thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) and free T4 as the initial tests. Subsequent evaluation may include ultrasound imaging, radioactive iodine uptake test (RAIU), and thyroid autoantibodies (see ). C
Treatment is based on etiology. Mild symptoms may be monitored, while NSAIDs or high-dose acetylsalicylic acid are first line for mild pain and inflammation associated with sub-acute thyroiditis. C
Patients with suppurative thyroiditis should be treated urgently with intravenous antibiotic therapy and, if indicated, surgical drainage of the abscess. C
Annual TSH testing should be done in women with a prior history of postpartum thyroiditis to evaluate for the development of permanent hypothyroidism. C
Thyroiditis is a group of disorders characterized by an inflammatory process of the thyroid gland, which can be due to bacterial infection, viral infection, or autoimmunity.

The patient might or might not have symptoms of inflammation; thyroid hormone levels vary for each subtype of the condition and stage of the disease. When it occurs within 12 months of a pregnancy, it is usually due to postpartum thyroiditis.
Chronic autoimmune thyroiditis (Hashimoto's): 0.3 to 1.5 cases/1000 persons/year.
Sub-acute thyroiditis: 4.9 cases/100,000 persons/year.
Riedel thyroiditis: 1.6 cases/100,000 persons/year.
Postpartum thyroiditis: overall estimated prevalence of 5.7% in the United States.
Acute suppurative thyroiditis: uncommon, 0.1% to 0.7% of all thyroid disease.
Hashimoto thyroiditis is one of the most common causes of autoimmune disorders and hypothyroidism in the Western world. Prevalence is higher in women than in men.

Patients with Hashimoto thyroiditis have an increased risk of developing thyroid cancer (RR 1.6, 95% CI 1.3–21.9) breast cancer (RR 1.7, 95% CI 1.3-3.2 and OR 2.6, 95% CI 1.9-3.4), and digestive organs cancer (RR 2.8, 95% CI 1.5–5.2).

Acute suppurative thyroiditis is most commonly caused by bacteria, such as Staphylococcus aureus, Salmonella, Klebsiella, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Pneumocystis jirovecii, Aspergillus, and Nocardia have been reported in immune-compromised patients.

Subacute thyroiditis has been associated with viral infections. Enterovirus is the cause in a large proportion of cases; Echovirus, Coxsackievirus A and B, mumps virus, Cytomegalovirus, Influenza A virus (H1N1 subtype), and Adenovirus have also been reported.
Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (COVID-19) has also been reported as associated with subacute thyroiditis but there is no evidence of a causal relationship.

Postpartum thyroiditis
Riedel thyroiditis
Silent thyroiditis (painless, subacute, lymphocytic thyroiditis)

Amiodarone can cause thyroiditis due to either iodine excess in a patient with latent or pre-existing thyroid disease (thyrotoxicosis I and hypothyroidism) or a destructive inflammatory process (thyrotoxicosis II).
Other drugs reported to cause thyroiditis include lithium, denileukin, interferon alfa, interleukin-2, and tyrosine kinase inhibitors.

Autoimmune thyroiditis is both T-cell and B-cell mediated. Thyroid antigen-specific helper T cells cause destruction through various means including activating cytotoxic T cells, resulting in apoptosis or triggering an autoimmune response inducing B cells to secrete thyroid antibodies. The most frequent antibodies are against thyroid peroxidase (TPOAb) and thyroglobulin (anti-thyroglobulin antibody, TgAB) both of which have the ability to cause complement fixation resulting in toxicity and cell destruction with subsequent lymphocytic infiltration of the thyroid gland. Antibodies blocking thyrotropin (TSH) receptors (TSH receptor-blocking antibodies, TBAb) have also been reported in patients with Hashimoto's thyroiditis.

A combination of genetic susceptibility and non-genetic factors has been proposed as a trigger for developing autoimmune thyroiditis: Thyroid-specific genes encode 2 autoantigens; thyroglobulin and the TSH receptor (TSHR). Genetic mutations such as those occurring in the autoimmune regulator (AIRE) gene or the FOXP3 gene responsible for the normal functioning of the regulatory T cells may cause failure to present thyroid antigen correctly in the thymus, resulting in loss of self-tolerance. On their own, these genetic mutations may not be enough to cause autoimmune destruction, but in combination with non-genetic factors, they are able to trigger an autoimmune event. Genetic polymorphism has been found in different ethnic groups with thyroiditis, although the real number of genetic loci that contribute to the development of Hashimoto disease is uncertain. Some genetic polymorphisms associated with autoimmune thyroiditis include major histocompatibility complex (MHC) genes (human leukocyte antigen [HLA]) that may determine cell-mediated destruction or autoantigen presentation and CD40 and CD226 genes that encode antigens and activate receptors on natural killer cells. Non-genetic factors contributing to the development of autoimmune thyroiditis include dietary factors such as iodine excess, vitamin D and selenium deficiency, toxins like polychlorinated biphenyl, low-dose irradiation, and drugs.

Acute suppurative thyroiditis is uncommon due to the encapsulation and high vascularity of the thyroid gland. It is rarely caused through direct infection of the gland; more often, it is due to abscess formation and fistulous connection. Extension of an internal fistula from the pyriform sinus is commonly seen in children.

Sub-acute thyroiditis is a cell-mediated inflammatory process. Viral infections have various means for triggering the disease process, including inflammatory destruction of thyroid follicles, induction of apoptosis, infiltration and disruption of the basal membrane, and subsequent rupture of the follicle. Preformed free T4 and free T3 are released to the blood stream, suppressing TSH during the thyrotoxic phase, which may last 4 to 8 weeks. After this phase, hypothyroidism may develop. Other means include formation of altered antigens and induction of aberrant HLA expression. This has been reinforced by reports of familial sub-acute thyroiditis, where HLA B35 was positive.

Postpartum thyroiditis is a transient or permanent elevation of thyroid function within 1 year of delivery. It is usually a result of immune-mediated destruction of the thyroid, causing release of preformed hormones initially, and generating a hyperthyroid phase, followed by hypothyroidism after depletion of the thyroid hormone stores.

Riedel thyroiditis results from limited or extensive fibrosis of the thyroid tissue with mononuclear infiltration of unknown etiology, although findings of thyroid antibodies suggest autoimmune mechanism of injury.
There is insufficient evidence to recommend screening nonpregnant asymptomatic adults for thyroid dysfunction (USPSTF I recommendation, 2015). C
There is insufficient evidence to recommend screening all women for postpartum thyroiditis. C
Corticosteroid therapy in patients with subacute thyroiditis achieves symptomatic relief but does not prevent early- or late-onset thyroid dysfunction. C

A systematic review of 15 studies but including only two RCTs concluded that low initial oral doses of steroids (15 mg/day prednisolone) followed by a prolonged tapering period may help prevent recurrence of subacute thyroiditis.

Retrospective studies of 522 females with over 2000 blood samples suggest that the presence of thyroid antibodies correlates with the development of autoimmune thyroiditis, even preceding the diagnosis of autoimmune thyroiditis by 5 to 7 years. This is true for anti-thyroid peroxidase antibodies (TPOAb), with an odds ratio of 19.1 for later development of autoimmune thyroiditis, and for thyroglobulin antibodies (TgAb), with an odds ratio of 78.
Transmission of TPOAb in chronic autoimmune thyroiditis is familial with a dominant trait seen in females but not males.

High prevalence of TPOAb in patients with some disorders has been associated with risk for autoimmune thyroiditis. Type 1 diabetes: prevalence of TPOAb is 16.9% in a series of 17,749 patients. Turner syndrome: 83% compared to 33% seen in other karyotypes were positive for TPOAb. Familial Alzheimer's disease: a small retrospective study (N = 70) reported that 41% of family members were TPOAb positive. This study was able to establish genetic cosegregation between the presence of TPOAb and the development of Alzheimer's disease.
Certain genetic predisposition: HLA alleles A, B, -DR, and -DQ have also been associated with increased risk for autoimmune thyroiditis.

A study carried out on children and adolescents from Belarus who had been exposed to the Chernobyl radioactive fallout concluded that previous exposure to radiation is associated with increased risk for autoimmune thyroiditis (19.5% exposed in utero compared to 3.8% of an unexposed group).
One systematic review of 587 studies including 8081 patients reported the prevalence of postpartum thyroiditis in patients with type 1 diabetes mellitus as 19.6% (95% CI 19.5%-19.7%).
Iodine deficiency, administration, and iodine-related contrast exposure have variable effects on the thyroid gland.
Consider thyroiditis in patients presenting with firm painless goiter; fever, dysphagia, dysphonia, or anterior neck pain; and hoarseness, dyspnea, stridor, or dysphagia. C
Initial evaluation for the patient with clinically suspected thyroiditis includes TSH and free T4. C

Use an algorithmic approach that involves selective use of radioactive iodine uptake (RAIU) scan, thyroid autoantibodies, and evaluation for suppurative thyroiditis in patients with signs of infection (). C
Ultrasound-guided fine needle aspiration (FNA) is recommended if acute suppurative thyroiditis is suspected. C

list.listitem: Consider thyroiditis in patients presenting with firm painless goiter; fever, dysphagia, dysphonia, or anterior neck pain; and hoarseness, dyspnea, stridor, or dysphagia.

Authors of a systematic review identified 8 local symptoms related to Hashimoto thyroiditis: neck pain (0.02%-16%), voice changes (7%-30%), throat discomfort (20%-44%), shortness of breath (28%-50%), dysphagia (29%), goiter-related symptoms (69%), sleep apnea, and generally defined compressive symptoms.
On examination, the thyroid gland may be tender to palpation.
See for typical history and physical examination findings of different types of thyroiditis.

When thyroid disease is clinically suspected, TSH and free T4 should be ordered as the initial test. TSH measurement has the highest sensitivity in evaluation of thyrotoxicosis symptoms. Its accuracy improves when free T4 and total T3 are assessed at the initial evaluation. In patients presenting in thyrotoxic state, initial diagnostic testing could include measurement of anti-thyroid receptor antibodies (TRAb), determination of radioactive iodine uptake (RAIU), and measurement of thyroidal blood flow and ultrasonography.

If there is a non-tender goiter, anti-thyroid peroxidase antibodies (TPOAb) should be ordered. A significant elevation of TPOAb is fairly specific for Hashimoto autoimmune thyroiditis. However, it can also be elevated in postpartum thyroiditis and sub-acute lymphocytic thyroiditis, both of which have an autoimmune etiology. Combining with thyroglobulin increases the sensitivity to 74% with a specificity of 86%.

In patients with suppurative thyroiditis, obtain a complete blood count (CBC) to evaluate leukocytosis and left shift, as well as an ESR. RAIU scan can help to differentiate between suppurative thyroiditis and sub-acute thyroiditis. Ultrasound and CT scan can be done in the early phase to look for abscess or fistula, but it may fail to differentiate between them, in which case consider ultrasound-guided fine needle aspiration (FNA). FNA with culture is the most accurate test for differential diagnosis when thyrotoxicosis is present.
If subacute thyroiditis is suspected, TSH, free T4, TPOAb, and TgAb should be ordered.

Color flow Doppler ultrasound can help to differentiate between Graves' disease with hypervascularization and sub-acute thyroiditis but is rarely necessary. In the latter, the gland is hypoechogenic with normal or low vascularity.
Sonographic elastography is indicated if there is stiffness of the thyroid gland, and neck CT scan if there are obstructive symptoms to differentiate Riedel's thyroiditis.
Riedel's thyroiditis requires histopathological confirmation. Minimally invasive (tru-cut) needle biopsy, open biopsies, or decompressive thyroidectomy are indicated.

The 24-hour RAIU is not helpful to establish the diagnosis of Hashimoto's thyroiditis. It is typically normal, low, or absent in patients with suppurative thyroiditis, sub-acute thyroiditis, drug-induced thyroiditis, and postpartum thyroiditis.
Measurement of the thyroidal blood flow and ultrasonography can be used when RAIU is contraindicated, such as during pregnancy or breastfeeding.
See for a suggested approach to the evaluation of the patient with clinically suspected thyroiditis.

Treatment is based on etiology. An NSAID or high-dose acetylsalicylic acid is the first-line treatment for mild pain and inflammation associated with sub-acute thyroiditis. Rarely, short-term oral corticosteroids may be necessary in the patient with severe symptoms. C

Most patients with painless thyroiditis do not need treatment for thyroid symptoms because they are mild and self-limiting. If symptoms are severe, treatment is targeted at management of hyper- or hypothyroid symptoms. C

Ultrasound-guided fine needle aspiration (FNA) with gram stain and culture should be peformed on patients with severe symptoms who are suspected of having suppurative thyroiditis, with appropriate antibiotics and drainage carried out immediately. C

Sub-acute thyroiditis: As this is typically self-limited, the goal is provision of symptomatic relief. NSAIDs and high-dose acetylsalicylic acid are first line. For more severe or persistent symptoms, consider use of glucocorticoids, 40 mg/day tapered over 4 to 6 weeks. However, in an RCT of 60 patients with subacute thyroiditis and moderate-severe pain unresponsive to NSAIDs, low dose prednisolone at 15 mg/d was noninferior to 30 mg/d for pain relief and complete resolution with a similar mean duration of treatment of mean duration of 34.62 ± 14.12 and 41.18 ± 16.89 days, respectively.

Drug-induced thyroiditis: Treatment depends on the type of drug and reaction. Generally, treat hyperthyroid symptoms with appropriate doses of anti-thyroid medications such as methimazole and beta blockers. A small prospective randomized trial of patients with type 2 amiodarone-induced thyroiditis concluded that oral corticosteroids (30 mg daily for 2 week with gradual taper over 3 months) were effective. Hypothyroidism should be treated with levothyroxine sodium replacement.

Chronic autoimmune thyroiditis (Hashimoto's): Some patients remain euthyroid; treatment with levothyroxine is indicated only if the patient is hypothyroid. The recommended starting dose in the general population is 1.6 mcg/kg and 0.5 mcg/kg for older individuals.

Suppurative (infectious) thyroiditis: Patients should be treated with immediate targeted IV antibiotic therapy with surgical drainage of abscess, if present. The first-line option for empiric therapy is a penicillinase-resistant penicillin and beta-lactamase inhibitor, such as nafcillin. Piperacillin/tazobactam or vancomycin may be used in patients suspected to have methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA) infection. Other options include penicillin or ceftriaxone with or without gentamicin. Clindamycin is recommended if the patient is allergic to penicillin.

Postpartum thyroiditis: Symptoms are typically mild. Monitor with repeat testing in 4 to 8 weeks or if new symptoms arise. Severe cases may require a short course of beta-blockers during the hyperthyroid phase, as these patients may progress through various phases. Women with elevated TSH who are attempting pregnancy or symptomatic women should be treated with levothyroxine.

Invasive fibrous thyroiditis (Riedel's thyroiditis): Anti-inflammatory treatment with glucocorticoids is the first-line therapy early in the disease. Mycophenolate and tamoxifen may also be used early in the disease or in combination with prednisone. Definitive treatment is surgical; debulking to relieve constricting effects or total thyroidectomy is recommended. Treat hypothyroid symptoms with levothyroxine and associated hypocalcemia with calcium supplementation.

Silent (painless) sporadic thyroiditis: Monitor asymptomatic patients as symptoms are usually mild and may be self-limiting. Beta-blockers are first-line therapy for patients with severe symptoms during the hyperthyroid phase, and levothyroxine is first line for patients with symptomatic hypothyroidism.
Radiation thyroiditis: Generally self-limited. Treat symptomatically, if needed, with beta-blockers and NSAIDs.
The most common indication for surgery is in patients with autoimmune thyroiditis and a coexisting thyroid nodule with cytology suspicious for malignancy.

Surgery may be indicated in select patients with chronic autoimmune thyroiditis. Within a subgroup of 150 patients aged 18-79 years who were euthyroid on medical therapy but had persistently severe symptoms and markedly elevated TPOab (>1000 IU/ml), improvement in symptom scores and TPOab titers was demonstrated in patients randomized to total thyroidectomy compared to control group at 6, 12 and 18 months.

Surgery is also indicated for relief of obstructive symptoms, such as seen in Riedel's thyroiditis. In such patients, debulking surgery (isthmusectomy) is recommended over total thyroidectomy due to the high rate of complications. One small retrospective review of all cases of patients with invasive fibrous thyroiditis (IFT) at Mayo Clinic, Rochester, from 1976 to 2008, demonstrated high rates of surgical complications. Of the 19 patients who had total thyroidectomy, 7 (39%) had surgical complications involving the vocal cords and parathyroid glands, and 2 required tracheostomies.

Infectious thyroiditis may require open surgical drainage of a thyroid gland abscess. Indications for surgery are clinical deterioration; persistent or non-resolving abscess, either on imaging or more than two ultrasound-guided FNA without improvement; or progression of the abscess or fistula formation.

Acupuncture as an adjunct to levothyroxine significantly reduced thyroid antibody and TSH levels in patients with Hashimoto thyroiditis compared to levothyroxine alone based on a meta-analysis of 14 Chinese RCTs with 1020 patients.

Small RCTs have suggested that selenium supplementation for treatment of autoimmune thyroiditis may be beneficial, but a Cochrane Systematic Review concluded that the evidence for or against efficacy of selenium supplementation in people with Hashimoto's thyroiditis is incomplete and that further well-randomized studies need to be done.

Authors of a more recent systematic review and meta-analysis of 35 RCTs concluded that selenium supplementation was effective and safe in lowering TSH and TPOAb levels in patients with Hashimoto thyroiditis who were not on thyroid replacement therapy.

Patients with sub-acute, silent, and postpartum thyroiditis presenting with mild symptoms may be monitored without treatment, as return to euthyroid state generally occurs within 12 to 18 months. Progression to overt hypothyroidism may occur in up to 25% of these patients.

In patients with postpartum thyroiditis in whom levothyroxine is initiated, gradual tapering can begin by 12 months postpartum with TSH monitoring every 6 to 8 weeks to determine if the patient has developed permanent hypothyroidism and needs lifelong replacement therapy.
There is no consensus on the optimal duration of antibiotics therapy for patients with suppurative thyroiditis.
In patients with suppurative thyroiditis, hospitalization and IV antibiotics are indicated as first-line therapy.
Severe symptoms requiring airway or cardiac monitoring.
Surgical referral is indicated following biopsy with suspicion for malignancy.

Monitor airway and cardiac status for acute compromise in patients suspected to have suppurative thyroiditis. Monitor and treat sepsis with appropriate IV antibiotics. Transient vocal cord paralysis may occur as a result of infection.
Chronic autoimmune thyroiditis has long been associated with a higher risk of papillary thyroid cancer, for which surgical referral would be indicated following nodule biopsy confirmation.
Consider opportunistic infections and use broad-spectrum guideline appropriate antibiotic therapy in patients with documented or suspected HIV infection.

The likelihood of full recovery depends on the etiology of the thyroiditis, TSH, and TPOAb levels. A 10-year prospective study demonstrated that the strongest risk factor for development of overt permanent thyroid failure from subclinical hypothyroid states is the level of TSH. The estimated incidence of overt hypothyroidism was 0% for TSH 4 to 6 mU/L, 42.8% for TSH >6 to 12 mU/L, and 76.9% for >12 mU/L after 10 years.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 18 cohort studies of patients with subacute thyroiditis found a recurrence rate of 12.0% (95% CI 8.2%-17.1%). The risk of recurrence in those treated with glucocorticoids was higher than that in the NSAIDs group (RR 1.84, 95% CI 1.04-3.24).
Monitoring for progression to overt hypothyroidism should be done in all patients with subclinical hypothyroidism who have elevated TPOAb levels.

Patients on drugs known to cause thyroid dysfunction such as amiodarone, lithium, interferon-alpha, and interleukin-2 should have thyroid function monitored while on these medications and every 6 months thereafter for at least 1 year.
Annual TSH testing should be considered in women with a prior history of postpartum thyroiditis to evaluate for the development of permanent hypothyroidism.
In patients with postpartum thyroiditis in whom levothyroxine is initiated, monitor and adjust dose every 4 to 8 weeks until euthyroidism is achieved.
Small RCTs suggest that there is no benefit to thyroid supplementation in older patients without overt thyroid failure.
For patients ≥65 years with a history of cardiovascular disease presenting with overt thyroid failure, levothyroxine should be started at 25-50 mcg/day and titrated.

Postpartum thyroiditis, defined as thyroid dysfunction within 12 months of delivery, includes transient autoimmune thyroiditis which is found in approximately 5% to 10% of women during the first year after childbirth. The thyrotoxic phase usually lasts only a few months and affected women are usually only mildly symptomatic. While most cases of postpartum thyroiditis resolve spontaneously, overt hypothyroidism can occur, most often between 4 and 8 months postpartum.

American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) 2020 guidelines recommend that physicians be aware of the risk factors and symptoms of postpartum thyroid dysfunction and evaluate patients when indicated.

In a pregnant woman with thyroid dysfunction, there is strong evidence supporting an increased risk for maternal and fetal complications such as preterm delivery and spontaneous pregnancy loss. Therefore, monitoring and fetal surveillance is recommended.

ACOG 2020 does not recommend universal screening for thyroid disease in pregnancy as identification and treatment of maternal subclinical hypothyroidism does not improve pregnancy or neonatal outcomes.
There is insufficient evidence to recommend iodine supplementation for women during conception, pregnancy, or the postpartum period.
Consult an experienced obstetrician or maternal-fetal medicine specialist for thyroid dysfunction in pregnancy, including presence of thyroid autoantibodies.
